title: Brief History of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, 1819–1953
excerpt: A comprehensive historical account of the State of Jammu and Kashmir from the Sikh conquest of 1819 to the political upheavals of 1953, tracing its formation, governance, diversity, legal structures, and the origins of the modern dispute.
author: Sardar Nasir Aziz Khan

heroImage.caption: Historical evolution of the State of Jammu and Kashmir.

body.text: Early Political Shifts Before 1846

In 1819, the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh defeated the Afghan Durrani rulers and took control of Kashmir. From 1819 to 1846, the Kashmir Valley remained under Sikh rule. During this period, Gulab Singh emerged as a key Dogra military leader and expanded his authority over Jammu and surrounding hill regions.

Throughout the 1820s and 1830s, forces under Gulab Singh extended control into Ladakh and Baltistan, laying the territorial foundations of a future mountain state encompassing Jammu, Kashmir Valley, Ladakh, and the northern frontier.
Treaty of Lahore and Treaty of Amritsar, 1846

The First Anglo‑Sikh War (1845–1846) resulted in the defeat of the Sikh Empire. Under the Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846), the Sikh government ceded territories to the British and was required to pay 15 million Nanakshahi rupees as war indemnity. Unable to pay the full amount, the Lahore Darbar accepted Gulab Singh’s offer to pay seventy‑five lakh Nanakshahi rupees.

On 16 March 1846, the Treaty of Amritsar was signed. The British transferred to Maharaja Gulab Singh all hilly and mountainous territories between the Indus and Ravi rivers, including Chamba. This treaty formally created the State of Jammu and Kashmir, with Gulab Singh as its founding ruler.
Rulers of the State (1846–1953)
Governance and Legal Reforms

Under Maharaja Ranbir Singh, administration was consolidated. The Ranbir Penal Code became the foundation of criminal law. District courts were established, judicial procedures formalized, and a professional Bar developed in Jammu and Srinagar. In 1928, the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir was formally established.
Infrastructure, Forests, and Ecological Management

Under Maharaja Pratap Singh, roads, public buildings, and communication systems expanded. Forest conservation was a major governance priority. More than 40% of the territory historically remained under forest cover. Cutting of valuable trees such as maple, pine, and deodar required state permission, and unauthorized felling was punishable.

Water systems—springs, canals, and irrigation channels—were maintained. Grazing lands were allocated, migration routes for herders recognized, and special pathways marked to prevent disputes and preserve ecological balance.
State Subject Rule of 1927

Maharaja Hari Singh introduced the State Subject Rule in 1927, defining hereditary state subjects and granting them exclusive rights to land ownership, government employment, and settlement. This safeguarded the State’s land, culture, identity, and economic rights from outside acquisition.
Praja Sabha and Constitutional Developments

In 1934, the Praja Sabha was established as the legislative assembly. It combined elected and nominated members, introducing limited franchise based on property, taxation, and education. In 1939, the assembly was expanded, strengthening legislative representation.

Education in state schools became free. Legal reforms prohibited marriage of minor girls below sixteen. Revenue and public service administration improved. Compared to many princely states, Jammu and Kashmir had advanced governance structures, codified laws, and defined citizenship.
Religious and Regional Diversity

The State was marked by diversity: a Muslim‑majority population overall, Hindu‑majority Jammu, and Buddhist‑majority Ladakh. Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists, and Sikhs lived with long traditions of coexistence and shared social and economic life.
Partition of 1947 and the Tribal Invasion

At partition, princely states could join India or Pakistan or remain independent. Maharaja Hari Singh chose independence. On 22 October 1947, Pakistani‑backed tribal forces invaded from the northwest. After Britain declined assistance, the Maharaja sought help from India, which required accession. He signed the Instrument of Provisional Accession limited to defense, foreign affairs, and communications.

Indian troops were airlifted to Srinagar with assurances to protect life, liberty, and property and to reunite the State. The invasion forced the Maharaja to leave Srinagar for Jammu. He never returned to rule from Srinagar and later went into exile.
United Nations Involvement

In 1948, the United Nations intervened. UNCIP resolutions required Pakistan to withdraw from the State’s territory—a requirement never fully met. India’s pledges to protect rights and allow the people to determine their future were also not fully realized.
Human Rights and the Divided State

The State remains disputed. Millions of Kashmiris are divided by the Line of Control, with restricted movement and separated families. These conditions raise concerns under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including Articles 1, 3, 9, 13, 17, and 21.
International Recognition of the Dispute

UN Military Observers remain on both sides of the ceasefire line. The European Parliament Resolution of 24 May 2007 and the OHCHR reports of 2018 and 2019 reaffirm that the Kashmir issue remains on the global agenda.
Historical Continuity and Contemporary Claims

India, Pakistan, and political parties across all regions of the divided State claim the same historical entity created on 16 March 1846. Without the Treaty of Amritsar, there would be no unified legal or historical basis linking the regions now administered separately.

From 1846 until the upheavals of 1947, the State existed with defined borders, citizenship laws, courts, a High Court, a Bar, a legislative assembly, protected forests, regulated grazing, water management, and structured governance. This historical State remains central to understanding the present and future of Jammu and Kashmir.
